summary: GPU rush-hour: noisy pod spillover causing request queue starvation and sustained p95 regressions
description:
Issue summary:
During the customer's peak traffic window (09:00-11:30 UTC) on 2026-03-10, Nimbus Health observed a sustained increase in p95 latency across their dedicated pool accompanied by timeouts for streaming requests. The behaviour correlated with sudden bursts of short, high-concurrency jobs from co-located tenant pods, which appear to be spilling over GPU resources and causing queue starvation for long-lived inference sessions.

Impact:
- Customer experiencing increased p95 latency from ~220ms to 1.8s for generation calls with streaming enabled.
- Intermittent 504/timeout responses for streams and some 5xx spikes.
- Apparent request backlog increases on pool head nodes leading to autoscaler not adding capacity quickly enough.

Environment:
- Dedicated GPU pool (ded-reserv-48) backing Nimbus Health dedicated tenant.
- Instance type: p4d.24xlarge equivalent.
- Region: us-east-1.
- Model variants in use: redwood/gpt-medium-v1 quantized and open/llama-3-7b fp16.

Steps to reproduce (observed pattern):
1) Schedule multiple short low-latency batched jobs from noisy tenant around rush window (synthetic reproduced using 200 concurrent 8-token requests across 30 pods).
2) Notice sustained rise in scheduler queue length and token-generation latency for long-running streaming sessions.
3) Autoscaler observes CPU/GPU metrics but does not scale fast enough due to conservative scaling policy and delayed GPU allocation.
4) Some inference sessions hit head-of-line queueing and get closed by client after 30s.

Logs / Metrics snippets:
- Serving-runtime queue depth spike: host-prod-rt-07 09:12 UTC - queue_length 120 -> 840 over 7 minutes.
- GPU util saw short spikes to 98% with rapid context-switching; observed repeated kernel preemption logs in node kubelet.
- Autoscaler events: "scale_up_suppressed" logged twice due to min-node-granularity policy.
- Customer-side traces show streaming keepalive disconnects at TCP level concurrent with queue peaks.

Immediate business risk: High - client workflows (clinical note generation) degraded, impacting SLAs and customer confidence.
investigation_notes:
Hypotheses: 1) Noisy short-burst pods from neighbor tenant are causing frequent GPU context switches, preventing the serving runtime from achieving steady KV cache warm state. 2) Autoscaler policy is mis-sized for the workload burst profile (min-granularity and cooldown too aggressive). 3) Scheduler bin-packing led to co-location of bursty pods on same head nodes as streaming workers.

What we checked so far:
- Correlated pod create/delete events with queue spikes; multiple bursty pods launched at 09:05 and 09:11.
- Kernel logs show MIG slice thrashing and repeated CUDA context initialization messages.
- Checked autoscaler logs: scale decision deferred because scaling metric was GPU memory pressure (which did not exceed threshold) while queue latency increased; threshold tuning needed.
- Confirmed tenant resource requests/limits: noisy tenant had low GPU memory request but high CPU and short runtimes, causing frequent scheduling churn.

Temporary mitigation applied:
- Manually evicted 6 noisy pods and cordoned two over-subscribed nodes at 09:40; p95 returned to ~300ms over 10 minutes.
- Increased autoscaler aggressiveness for the dedicated pool (lowered cooldown from 300s to 120s) as a safety-level override for the next 48h.

Open actions for Eng/SRE:
- Adjust scheduler bin-packing policy to prefer isolation of streaming sessions from short-burst jobs.
- Add autoscaler reflex policy to react to queue length and p95 latency signals (not just GPU mem).
- Add quota/enforcement rule to restrict per-tenant burst concurrency on shared heads or prefer dedicated GPU slices for noisy tenants.
- Run a capacity planning simulation for worst-case burst profiles.
resolution:
Workaround and temporary fixes applied to stabilize customer during incident window: manual noisy-pod eviction and node cordon; autoscaler cooldown reduced and temporary reflex scaling on queue-length enabled. Longer-term actions assigned to SRE and Scheduler teams. Customer notified of mitigations and timeline.

Follow-up actions (owner -> ETA):
- Scheduler isolation policy change (owner: Priya Nair) -> 2026-03-20.
- Autoscaler policy patch to include queue-length signal (owner: Marco Silva) -> 2026-03-18.
- Tenant burst quota enforcement improvements (owner: Security/Policy team) -> 2026-04-02.
- Post-incident capacity run and runbook update (owner: Jonah Kramer) -> 2026-03-17.
